Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-04 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Kim (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (CTO, Cobalt Edge), Lina Gomez (Head of ML), Tom Reeves (VP Eng)

Summary:
High-level pilot scoping to align on success criteria (latency / cost / quality), workload sizing (avg tokens/request, QPS), benchmark plan (models to run, hardware), and budget + timeline for a 2-3 week pilot. Security and VPC requirements discussed; customer to provide sample data.

Topics covered: success criteria, throughput targets, per-token cost targets, batching and prefix/KV caching, pilot timeline and budget, security knobs (KMS, SSO), benchmark logistics.

[00:00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through a tight scoping session for the unit economics pilot. Jonah and I will run bench config and Maia, sorry I mean Maya — oh sorry — auto-correct, ok —
[00:00:18] Rajiv: No worries. So our main goal, we get a smaller pilot to validate cost per user event. We're trying to figure out if Redwood can meet our p95 latency target and stay under our monthly inference budget.
[00:00:36] Lina: Quick context — typical request is the conversational summary use case, average input + response ~2k tokens combined but heavy tail up to 6k, about 40% of requests are short ( <300 tokens ). Current production load is roughly 20QPS peak, expected to double in 6 months.
[00:00:56] Tom: And budget — we have an initial runway of $25k for the pilot phase, and if we see good unit economics we'll look at reserved capacity.
[00:01:12] Jonah: Great, that helps. For the pilot we typically recommend 2-week bench runs plus a short integration window. We'll size the bench around peak QPS to simulate tails. A few quick questions: what is your success criteria — is it strictly p95 latency, or do you have quality thresholds too?
[00:01:31] Rajiv: Main go/no-go is p95 < 200ms for the short responses and <500ms for long generation, but that's flexible if cost is much better. Also, quality can't drop more than 5% on our eval metric (we use ROUGE-like summary score).
[00:01:48] Maya: Noted. From a unit cost perspective, what's your target per token or per request? Even ballpark helps us pick model variants + batching.
[00:02:02] Lina: We're aiming for under $0.001 per token effective, or roughly <$0.15 per request average. But that's tight; if Redwood can get us to $0.0006/token with similar quality we'd be very happy.
[00:02:18] Jonah: OK. To hit that kind of unit cost, we'll look at batching windows ~10-30ms, prefix KV caching for repeated prompts, and possibly mixed-precision or quantized variants. We'll propose an L2/L4 class GPU baseline and then a cheaper quantized run for cost comparison.
[00:02:34] Tom: Can you explain prefix cache impact in lay terms? Our engineering lead wants to understand tradeoffs.
[00:02:42] Jonah: Sure — prefix cache stores decoder KV states for repeated prefixes so you don't re-run the full context. For chat-heavy loads with repeated system prompts or repeated user patterns, cache hit rates of 30-60% can lower token compute by the same order. In bench we instrument cache hit/miss and simulate TTL. But, cache adds RAM and also needs sticky routing sometimes.
[00:03:06] Rajiv: Sticky routing is a concern — we run across multiple AZs and can't afford a single-node hotspot. What's Redwood's suggestion?
[00:03:14] Maya: We can do soft affinity with fallback; if a hot node is busy we route to a compatible model variant. For Dedicated deployments we can reserve a pool so you avoid cross-az latency jumps. We'll capture routing policies in the runbook.
[00:03:29] Lina: Security — we need KMS integration and audit logs for every request; also SSO + RBAC.
[00:03:36] Maya: Yep, SOC 2 is available, we support KMS/HSM, and can export request-level audit logs to your SIEM. We'll include the security pack in the follow-up.
[00:03:47] Jonah: Back to sizing — you mentioned 20QPS now, projected 40QPS in 6 months. For bench let's size to 50QPS to include headroom and tail risk. What's your average sequence length on generation vs embeddings?
[00:04:02] Lina: Generation average ~1.2k output tokens, input 800 tokens on average. Embeddings are a separate flow, smaller but high volume — maybe another 100 QPS for embedding calls.
[00:04:14] Jonah: Good, we'll include both flows. For embeddings we typically use batching more aggressively since latency constraints are softer. We'll estimate effective per-token cost separately for gen and embed.
[00:04:27] Tom: For hardware, are you planning to show comparisons between A100 and L40s, or quantized on cheaper chips?
[00:04:35] Jonah: We'll run three axes: fp16 on A100 (baseline perf), fp16 on L40s (latency/throughput diff), and 4-bit quantized on an efficient runtime (cost-optimized). We'll produce per-token cost numbers and a sensitivity table showing batching window vs latency vs unit cost.
[00:04:56] Rajiv: How do you calculate "per-token" — does that include orchestration overhead and cache misses?
[00:05:02] Jonah: We'll include all infra overheads visible to you — compute, GPU time, small infra (routing), and a normalized amortized cost per token. We'll show a breakdown: raw model computation, batching overhead, network, and caching delta.
[00:05:15] Lina: One more — can you instrument quality drift during quantized runs? Our worry is the 4-bit quality drop.
[00:05:22] Jonah: Yes, we'll run your eval set against each variant and produce regression alerts if quality drops beyond thresholds. We'll include sample outputs per-case in the bench artifacts.
[00:05:33] Maya: Timeline proposal: week 0 (this week) - sign SOW and exchange security docs; week 1 - integration + sample data ingestion; week 2 - run benchmark suite; week 3 - analyze results and decision. That's ~3 weeks. Does that match your expectations?
[00:05:48] Rajiv: Yes, 3 weeks is fine. We may want an optional extension to run a production canary if metrics look good.
[00:05:56] Tom: Regarding budget — $25k covers the bench compute and Redwood time? Any hidden costs?
[00:06:04] Maya: We'll put a pilot package in the SOW that includes 2-week bench compute + 10 hours of SE time + benchmarking report. If you want extended tuning or additional runs that's out of scope and we'll quote separately. We'll be explicit in the SOW to avoid surprises.
[00:06:18] Lina: For the bench, what does a typical configuration look like — number of parallel workers, batch sizes?
[00:06:24] Jonah: We simulate user concurrency with N workers per host, dynamic batching up to batch size 256 for embeddings and 32-64 for generation depending on token length. Batching window we tune in 10ms increments to hit latency SLOs. We also instrument tail latency hotspots.
[00:06:41] Rajiv: And caching TTL / eviction policy?
[00:06:45] Jonah: We'll test multiple TTLs; for chat we often see 30s-5min TTLs depending on session patterns. We'll report cache hit curves and the effective cost savings per hit rate scenario.
[00:06:58] Maya: On contract / legal — procurement wants an incoterm? — sorry that's wrong wording — they want standard enterprise terms; we can share templates.
[00:07:06] Tom: We'll need the security addendum and data processing agreement in advance.
[00:07:10] Maya: We'll attach both with the SOW.
[00:07:14] Rajiv: If we see good numbers, what's the path to Dedicated or Private? Can we move to reserved capacity with pinning model versions?
[00:07:21] Maya: Yes — pilot -> reserved Dedicated pool with monthly commit, and model pinning and rollout policies for safe upgrades. For Private we can discuss VPC/on-prem options if compliance requires air-gapped later.
[00:07:33] Lina: One more technical — for long-context generations we worry about KV cache memory blowup. Do you have memory-saving options?
[00:07:40] Jonah: We have selective KV eviction and block-sparse attention options on certain model families; part of the bench is to test memory footprint and pick the appropriate runtime knobs.
[00:07:52] Rajiv: Great. Are there any red flags from your side on our sample profile? The 6k tail could be expensive.
[00:07:58] Jonah: It's manageable in a bench; we'll show tail mitigation strategies: chunking, re-ranking, or offloading very long contexts to cheaper model variant for retrieval-augmented steps.
[00:08:10] Tom: Ok, let's talk instrumentation — we need per-route token-level cost and per-request tracing to integrate with our APM.
[00:08:18] Maya: Redwood Console can export token breakdown by model route, and tracing hooks for your tracer. We'll send a sample dashboard and the tracer integration guide.
[00:08:29] Lina: On evaluation — we'll share a 1k-case eval set for quality checks. Expect some noisy transcripts; our annotators will clean them but we'll give raw and cleaned.
[00:08:38] Rajiv: How long to run the bench once you have our sample data?
[00:08:41] Jonah: The run itself is about 4-8 hours per hardware variant if we run thorough sensitivity sweeps; but we'll parallelize where possible and aim to complete the bench in week 2.
[00:08:52] Maya: Recap / next steps: 1) Redwood sends SOW + security docs (Maya), 2) Cobalt Edge sends anonymized dataset + traffic profile (Rajiv), 3) Jonah schedules and runs benchmark and shares runbook, 4) results + cost sensitivity table delivered and review call.
[00:09:12] Tom: That works. Any other blockers?
[00:09:15] Lina: None from ML side. Just need confirmation on evaluation metrics format.
[00:09:19] Jonah: I'll include the exact metrics CSV schema in the runbook.
[00:09:23] Rajiv: Ok thanks, let's get SOW and security docs and we'll prioritize dataset export.
[00:09:28] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD with materials.
[00:09:32] Rajiv: Thanks.
